query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Partial substitution of Hf by vanadium in the HfMoTaTiZr alloy will reduce the overall density without significantly degrading its high strength at both room temperature and around 1000 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr with a density of approximately 10.21 g/cm³ and high strength maintained from room temperature to elevated temperatures (~1000 °C).
generation.intervention: Replace a portion (or all) of the heavy Hf with a lighter element such as V while keeping the other elements constant.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing and microstructural characterization performed at room temperature and at elevated temperature (~1000 °C) under relevant tensile and/or compressive loading conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Retention of a high-entropy, single-phase solid solution with preserved lattice distortion and phase stability, thereby maintaining solid-solution and precipitation strengthening mechanisms.
generation.mechanism: Substituting Hf (a heavy element driving high density) with V (a lighter element with comparable high-temperature performance) lowers the overall atomic weight. Provided the atomic size mismatch and bonding characteristics remain sufficiently compatible to retain a single-phase microstructure, the substitution can reduce density while preserving the mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: A measurable decrease in density (expected reduction potentially on the order of 10–20% in the heavy element’s contribution as substitution level increases) with a negligible (<10–15%) impact on yield strength at both room temperature and ~1000 °C, maintaining phase stability.
generation.baseline: The as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy's density (~10.21 g/cm³) and mechanical strength at room and elevated temperatures.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to as-cast or similarly processed alloys under mechanical loading and temperature conditions spanning room temperature to approximately 1000 °C. Phase stability and mechanical testing should be confined to conditions where the high-entropy structure is maintained.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal fraction of Hf that can be replaced by V without triggering deleterious phase transformations or a more significant loss in high-temperature strength is not precisely known and may depend on processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of alloys with varying levels of Hf substitution by V (e.g., 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100% replacement of Hf) using the same as-cast processing route as the original HfMoTaTiZr alloy. Characterize these alloys using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to assess phase stability and microstructure. Measure density and perform tensile or compression tests at room temperature and at 1000 °C.
measurements: XRD patterns for phase and lattice parameter analysis
Mechanical testing (yield strength, ultimate tensile/compressive strength) at room temperature and 1000 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if any V-substituted alloy exhibits either a significant drop (more than 10–15%) in yield strength compared to the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr or shows evidence of phase decomposition/deleterious phase formation under room temperature or elevated temperature testing.

SLM-built HEA had a face-centered cubic (FCC) single-phase random solid solution. In addition, SLM-built HEA was composed of epitaxial growth grains, dislocation network and nano-sized oxides. Room- and high-temperature compression tests confirmed that SLM-built HEA has outstanding mechanical properties in all temperature ranges compared to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEAs reported up to the present. The excellent mechanical properties of SLM-built HEA were achieved with fine grains, high dislocation density and fine precipitates at low temperatures (25 °C to 600 °C), and by high dislocation density and fine precipitates at high temperatures (700 °C or higher). On the other hand, the deformation microstructure showed that slip and deformation twins are the main deformation mechanisms from 25 °C to 600 °C, and slip and partial recrystallization are the main deformation mechanisms above 700 °C. Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ]. frame.system: The as‐cast high‐entropy alloy HfMoTaTiZr, which exhibits high strength at both room temperature and elevated temperatures (≈1000 °C) but has a high density (~10.21 g/cm³).
frame.goal: Reduce the overall density of the alloy without sacrificing its established mechanical properties across room temperature and elevated temperatures (≈1000 °C).
frame.limitation: The alloy’s current composition delivers excellent strength but at the expense of a relatively high density, limiting its attractiveness for lightweight high‐performance applications.
root_cause_cues: without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C
constraints: Must maintain high strength at both room temperature and elevated temperatures (≈1000 °C)
Intervention should not compromise high-temperature phase stability or lead to deleterious phase transformations
regime: Elevated temperature conditions up to approximately 1000 °C under service-relevant loading scenarios
prior_attempts: The as‐cast design itself (with all constituent elements in roughly equiatomic amounts) optimized for strength has been used, but it inherently includes heavy elements (notably Hf) that drive up the density.
frame.understanding: The proposed hypothesis leverages elemental substitution as a design intervention—specifically replacing a heavy constituent (Hf) with a lighter, high‐melting, and mechanically compatible element (for example, substituting Hf with V). The mechanism is that by reducing the atomic weight contribution while retaining the essential high-entropy and solid-solution strengthening effects (via maintained lattice distortion and electronic interactions), the overall density is reduced and strength is preserved. Directionally, one would expect a notable reduction in density (potentially in the range of 10–20% depending on the substitution level) while maintaining a similar yield strength and phase stability at room temperature and near 1000 °C. Prior studies in HEAs have demonstrated that strategic substitution with lighter elements (e.g., Al or V additions in other refractory HEAs) can successfully reduce density without a severe penalty in mechanical performance, provided that the substitution does not trigger deleterious phase transformations. An experiment to validate the hypothesis would involve preparing a series of alloys with incremental substitutions of Hf by V, followed by comprehensive microstructural (XRD, TEM) and mechanical (tensile/compression testing at room temperature and 1000 °C) characterization. A rejection criterion would be observing a significant deterioration (for instance, >10–15% decrease) in yield strength or the onset of undesirable phase formation at elevated temperatures relative to the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr.
